title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
Suno and Udio trained their music generation models on copyrighted songs scraped from the internet without permission. The companies were reportedly unclear about their training data sources, and when prompted with references to specific artists and songs, their systems generated outputs that replicated characteristics of well-known recordings. This represents a model trained on unlicensed copyrighted material deployed to generate new music, where the training process itself violated copyright law rather than just the outputs.

Record labels, independent artists, and publishing companies filed multiple lawsuits across jurisdictions, with some cases resulting in court rulings against Suno and settlement agreements with both companies and major labels. To catch this before deployment would have required either licensing the training data or obtaining explicit consent from copyright holders, and transparency about training sources that could withstand legal scrutiny.

It is not established whether the companies intentionally concealed their training methods or whether the generation of song-like outputs was an unavoidable technical outcome rather than a deliberate feature of the systems.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Atlantic Records, and Capitol Records, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two prominent AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and of directly reproducing sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits claim the companies have been deliberately unclear about their training data and argue that admitting the truth would expose willful copyright infringement on a massive scale.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated that they could repeatedly recreate versions of well-known songs by using specific prompts that reference song characteristics like decade, genre, and artist style. Examples include AI-generated songs that replicate the style of Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," Bill Haley's rockabilly sound, and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The record labels submitted thousands of copyrighted works they claim were used in training, featuring artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, and many others. The lawsuits, filed in New York and Massachusetts, represent a significant legal battle over how generative AI services can use existing creative works.
